content: Before initiating therapy with cefuroxime (Zinacef), it is essential to thoroughly assess whether the patient has a history of hypersensitivity reactions to cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. This medication should be administered cautiously to patients with a known sensitivity to penicillin. Antibiotics, including cefuroxime, should be used with caution in individuals with a history of any form of allergy, particularly drug allergies. If an allergic reaction to cefuroxime occurs, the drug must be discontinued immediately. Severe acute hypersensitivity reactions may necessitate the use of epinephrine and other emergency interventions. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefuroxime, and can range in severity from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibiotic treatment disrupts the normal flora of the colon, leading to an overgrowth of C. difficile. This bacterium produces toxins A and B, which contribute to the development of CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and could require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use. A detailed medical history is crucial, as CDAD has been reported to occur up to two months after the administration of antibacterial agents. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate management, including fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, targeted antibiotic therapy for C. difficile, and surgical evaluation, should be implemented as clinically indicated. In cases of severe or unresponsive colitis, oral vancomycin is the preferred treatment for antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis caused by C. difficile. Other potential causes of colitis should also be considered. Although cefuroxime rarely affects kidney function, renal status should be monitored during therapy, particularly in seriously ill patients receiving maximum doses. Cephalosporins should be used cautiously in patients receiving concurrent treatment with potent diuretics, as these regimens may adversely affect renal function. In patients with transient or persistent renal insufficiency, the total daily dose of cefuroxime should be reduced to prevent high and prolonged serum antibiotic concentrations. Prolonged use of cefuroxime, like other antibiotics, may lead to the overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms. Patients should be closely monitored, and appropriate measures should be taken if superinfection occurs during therapy. Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be prescribed cautiously in individuals with a history of gastrointestinal disease, particularly colitis. Nephrotoxicity has been reported with the concurrent administration of aminoglycoside antibiotics and cephalosporins. Mild-to-moderate hearing loss has been reported in some pediatric patients treated with cefuroxime for meningitis, as with other therapeutic regimens for this condition. Persistence of positive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cultures at 18 to 36 hours has been observed with cefuroxime injection and other antibiotic therapies, though the clinical significance of this finding is unclear. Cephalosporins may be associated with a reduction in prothrombin activity. Patients at risk include those with renal or hepatic impairment, poor nutritional status, prolonged courses of antimicrobial therapy, or those stabilized on anticoagulant therapy. Prothrombin time should be monitored in at-risk patients, and exogenous vitamin K should be administered as indicated. Prescribing cefuroxime in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or prophylactic indication is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Patients should be informed that antibacterial drugs, including cefuroxime, are intended to treat bacterial infections and are not effective against viral infections (e.g., the common cold). When prescribed cefuroxime for a bacterial infection, patients should be advised to take the medication exactly as directed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood of bacteria developing resistance, rendering them untreatable by cefuroxime or other antibacterial drugs in the future. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, patients should be advised to contact their physician if they develop watery and bloody stools (with or without stomach cramps and fever) even as late as two or more months after completing the antibiotic course. Cefuroxime, like other antibiotics, may alter gut flora, potentially reducing the efficacy of combined estrogen/progesterone oral contraceptives by lowering estrogen reabsorption. Patients should be counseled accordingly. False-positive results for glucose in the urine may occur with copper reduction tests (e.g., Benedict's or Fehling's solution, or CLINITEST® tablets) but not with enzyme-based tests for glycosuria. A false-negative result may occur with the ferricyanide test; therefore, glucose oxidase or hexokinase methods are recommended for determining blood plasma glucose levels in patients receiving cefuroxime. Cefuroxime does not interfere with the assay of serum and urine creatinine by the alkaline picrate method. Lifetime animal studies to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of cefuroxime have not been conducted. However, no mutagenic activity was observed in the mouse lymphoma assay or bacterial mutation tests. Positive results were obtained in an in vitro chromosome aberration assay, but negative results were found in an in vivo micronucleus test at doses up to 10 g/kg. Reproductive studies in animals have revealed no impairment of fertility. Cefuroxime is classified as Pregnancy Category B. Animal studies at doses up to 1.5 times the maximum recommended human dose (based on mg/m²) have shown no evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Because animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of human response, cefuroxime should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Since cefuroxime is excreted in human milk, caution should be exercised when administering it to nursing women. The safety and effectiveness of cefuroxime in pediatric patients below three months of age have not been established. Accumulation of other cephalosporins in newborns, resulting in prolonged drug half-life, has been reported. Of the 1,914 subjects who received cefuroxime in 24 clinical studies, 901 (47%) were aged 65 years and older, and 421 (22%) were aged 75 years and older. No overall differences in safety or effectiveness were observed between these subjects and younger patients. However, greater susceptibility to drug effects in some older individuals cannot be ruled out. Since cefuroxime is substantially excreted by the kidneys, the risk of toxic reactions may be greater in patients with impaired renal function. Elderly patients are more likely to have decreased renal function; therefore, dose selection should be cautious, and renal function should be monitored.
